name: Popcorn
seoDesc: Popcorn: work out portion size from the I'm serving and the cups of popcorn. A free food calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: portion size is what the Popcorn calculator works out, and it gets there from the I'm serving, the cups of popcorn and the calories. It suits portioning, timing or nutrition. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Popcorn calculator work?
sections.html:
The Popcorn calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports portion size in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the I'm serving, the cups of popcorn and the calories.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A number, expressed in people.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in 1 cup (~237 ml). The unit chip switches it to any of the 4 supported units.
  • A number, expressed in kcal/portion.

2 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.html:
Everything the page asks for and everything it reports, side by side. The roles matter: a value you supply is read from the form, a calculated value is derived from the others and cannot be set directly.

sections.title: The formula behind the Popcorn calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Portion size=cups of popcorn
Kernels needed=(5 ÷ 9) × I'm serving × cups of popcorn
Flavor=calories ÷ cups of popcorn

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
The form opens with a complete set of values: Portion size set to Standard portion and Flavor set to Air-popped popcorn. Straight away the calculator returns Cups of popcorn = 2 cups and Calories = 62.

Those are real numbers produced by the same engine that runs when you press Calculate, so you can change any single box afterwards and watch the answer move from this starting point.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Cups of popcorn = 2 cups and Calories = 62 should be roughly the size you expected from Portion size set to Standard portion and Flavor set to Air-popped popcorn.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• The option the calculation settles on.
  • Shown in tablespoons (15 ml), and convertible to any of the 14 units on that chip.
  • The option the calculation settles on.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Popcorn size, opening in 1 cup (~237 ml)
  • Kitchen volume measures, opening in tablespoons (15 ml)

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Popcorn calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking portions before you shop
  • Working out timing so everything finishes together
  • Scaling a recipe up or down
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the I'm serving, the cups of popcorn and the calories — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Popcorn calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns portion size, derived from the I'm serving, the cups of popcorn and the calories. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Popcorn calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the I'm serving, the cups of popcorn and the calories, which is 3 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter cups of popcorn in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Cups of popcorn opens in 1 cup (~237 ml) and the chip beside it offers 4 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Cups of popcorn = 2 cups. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Popcorn calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
